newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish exchequer seen in surplus, inflation a worry.
newsitem.headline: Irish exchequer seen in surplus, inflation a worry.

text.p: Ireland's Exchequer Borrowing figure is expected to show a large surplus again in July but inflation remains a concern as underlying credit is forecast to grow by up to 20 percent in June, economists said on Friday.
Next week sees the release of the July Exchequer Borrowing Requirement on Tuesday, June monthly credit growth data and the July Consumer Price Index on Thursday.
"The Exchequer showed a big surplus of 721 million punts in the six months to June and I think it will be a surplus of about 600 million in July," Riada economist Dan McLaughlin told Reuters.
McLaughlin said Ireland's continuing strong revenue growth should continue to boost the Exchequer's coffers.
"I am going for just under 0.3 percent for the CPI (consumer price index), similar to last month, that will give an 11 month increase of 1.6 percent," Bank of Ireland economist Jim Power said.
Consumer prices rose 0.3 percent in June from May, and were up 1.8 percent from May 1996. June 1996 data were not available.
Power said he expected a borrowing requirement of 150 million punts during the month, which would give a surplus of around 570 million for January-July.
"On private sector credit the underlying level will be around 19.5 percent," he added. Credit grew 18.9 percent in May.
Power said it would take a credit growth number in excess of 20 percent to bring nervousness back into the interest rate market.

"The market has pretty much discounted these kinds of numbers," Power said. "I think they will be more concerned about what is happening to sterling and in that regard next Thursday's monetary policy decision in the UK will be crucial."

NCB stockbrokers economist Dermot O'Brien said he expected Ireland's EBR to be in surplus to the tune of 500 million punts and saw credit growth rising to about 19 percent, boosted by borrowings incurred as a result of Norwich Union's recent flotation.
"The credit figure will remain strong, we are putting in 19 percent as a round number because Norwich Union borrowings would still be affecting it," O'Brien said.
O'Brien said he expected the CPI to show a 1.4 percent rise on an 11 month basis and to be up 0.2 percent on the month.
Bloxham's Alan McQuaid was forecasting a 600 million surplus for the Exchequer number and expected the monthly banking statistics to show underlying credit growth of about 20 percent.
"It will be a bad number but maybe not as strong as I originally thought, as some people will have paid back borrowings taken out to buy the Norwich shares," he said.
McQuaid expected mortgage lending up 14.6 percent year on year versus 14.4 percent last month.
On inflation McQuaid said the bigger risk to inflation in the near term was rises in service sector prices.

"Things such as VHI (Voluntary Health Insurance) increases, bus and rail fares going up, parking meter increases, those type of increases which are on the cards are more of a risk to inflation then the sterling exchange rate," he said.
